sentences.text: 2. The above case originated on a private complaint consequent to the filing of a refer report by the Police stating that the issue involved is civil nature.
The complainant before the Trial Court claims to be one of the partners of a Partnership Firm.

According to the complainant, the petitioner herein who conducts an institution of marketing had received an amount of Rs.40,00,000/- with the offer that the second respondent, who is the complainant herein, would be provided with a share of the profits obtained in the business being conducted, making use of the above amount.

It is also alleged that, as required by the petitioner, the defacto complainant had canvassed several friends and relatives of the defacto complainant and had made deposits with the establishment being conducted by the petitioner herein.

It is the further allegation that when there arose an issue with regard to the non-payment of the profits to the defacto complainant 2024:KER:93554 and the other persons who made deposits with the establishment of the petitioner, there was an understanding to transfer an amount of Rs.70,00,000/- to the petitioner by selling the property of the defacto complainant for the purpose of settling the claims of the persons, who invested in the business of the petitioner.
Thus, it is stated that the property belonging to the defacto complainant was sold and the amount of Rs.70,00,000/- so obtained was entrusted to the petitioner.

It is the further allegation of the second respondent that the petitioner issued a cheque for the repayment of the aforesaid amount of Rs.70,00,000/-, and that at the time of issuance of the above cheque, the account of the petitioner had already been frozen.

Thus, the second respondent approached the Trial Court with an allegation that, right from the very beginning, the petitioner was having the intention to defraud him and the other persons who made investments in the business conducted by the petitioner.

It is also alleged that the petitioner had misappropriated the amount of Rs.40,00,000/- entrusted by the second respondent believing the offer of the petitioner that the second respondent would be provided with the share of profits.
Heard the learned counsel for the petitioner, the learned counsel for the second respondent and the learned Public Prosecutor representing the State of Kerala.

4. It is submitted by the learned counsel for the second respondent that the case is now at the stage of pre-charge evidence before the Trial Court towards ascertaining the question whether there are sufficient grounds for framing a charge against the petitioner.
The learned counsel for the petitioner would argue that in the given set of facts of the case, none of the offences alleged against the petitioner are attracted.

It is further contended that the property entrusted with the petitioner was utilised in accordance with the understanding between the parties and hence it cannot be said that Praveen Gopalan vs State Of Kerala on 11 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/60263206/
2 there was any misappropriation or breach of trust.

sentences.text: It is also stated that there was no act committed by the petitioner deceiving the defacto complainant or any other persons, and hence the offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, is not attracted.

5. On going through the various averments in the complaint, it seems that the issue involved has to be analysed in detail after considering the records produced as well as the evidence let in by the 2024:KER:93554 defacto complainant to ascertain whether the offences alleged against the petitioner are made out or not.
It is true that there is, to a certain extent, some sort of contractual violation alleged against the petitioner giving it a colour of civil nature.

But that alone is not a ground to terminate the proceedings since there are many transactions in which the offence under cheating would be attracted notwithstanding the fact that there is also civil liability on the part of the persons who are bound to make payment to the complainant.

At any rate, it is not possible to terminate the prosecution proceedings at this stage in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 482 Cr.P.C., since the allegations against the petitioner would constitute the essential ingredients of cheating.
It would not be proper for this Court to analyse the case of the petitioner in the light of all probabilities in order to determine whether a conviction would be sustainable.

6. The following excerpt from the judgment of the Apex Court in V.Y. Jose v. State of Gujarat,
[(2009) 3 SCC 78] would be capable of elucidating the law in this regard with precision and clarity:

This Court, therein upon referring to Bhajan Lal [1992 Supp (1) SCC 335 : 1992 SCC (Cri) 426] opined as under: (Kishore Gupta case [(2004) 1 SCC 691 :
2004 SCC (Cri) 353] , SCC pp. 700-01, para 11) "11.
As noted above, the powers possessed by the High Court under Section 482 of the Code are very wide and the very plenitude of the power requires great caution in its exercise.
Court must be careful to see that its decision in exercise of this power is based on sound principles.
The inherent power should not be exercised to stifle a legitimate prosecution.

The High Court being the highest court of a State should normally refrain from giving a prima facie decision in a case where the entire facts are incomplete and hazy, more so, when the evidence has not been collected and produced before the Court and the issues involved, whether factual or legal, are of magnitude and cannot be seen in their true perspective without sufficient material.
Of course, no hard-and-fast rule can be laid down in regard to cases in which the High Court will exercise its extraordinary jurisdiction of quashing the proceedings at any stage.

(See Janata Dal v.
H.S. Chowdhary [(1992) 4 SCC 305 : 1993 SCC (Cri) 36] and Raghubir Saran (Dr.) v. State of Bihar [AIR 1964 SC 1] .)

sentences.text: In proceedings instituted on complaint, exercise of the inherent powers to quash the proceedings is called for only in a case where the complaint does not disclose any offence or is frivolous, vexatious or oppressive.

If the allegations set out in the complaint do not constitute the offence of which cognizance has been taken by the Magistrate, it is open to the High Court to quash the same in exercise of the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code.

It is not,
however, necessary that there should be meticulous analysis of the case before the trial to find out whether the case would end in conviction or acquittal.
The complaint has to be read as a whole.

If it appears that on consideration of the allegations in the light of the statement made on oath of the complainant that the ingredients of the offence or offences are disclosed and there is no material to show that the complaint is mala fide, frivolous or vexatious, in that event there would be no justification for interference by the High Court. When an information is lodged at the police station and an offence is registered, then the mala fides of the informant would be of secondary importance.
It is the material collected during the investigation and evidence led in the court which decide the fate of the accused person.

The allegations of mala fides against the informant are of no consequence and cannot by itself be the basis for quashing the proceedings."
(emphasis supplied) No exception can be taken to the aforementioned principles of law, as therein also it has categorically been held that exercise of inherent power under Section 482 is permissible where 2024:KER:93554 allegations set out in the complaint do not constitute the offence for which cognizance has been taken by the Magistrate."
7.
In the light of the aforesaid discussion, I find no reason to interfere with the proceedings pending before the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court, Irinjalakuda, in C.C.No.2121/2016.
